document.title: Transforming Public Digital Identity: A Blockchain Case in Action from the UN System
document.revision: UNJSPF/UNICC White Paper: Transforming Public Digital Identity, September 2025

chunks.heading: Foreword: purpose and design philosophy of the DCE
chunks.text: The UNJSPF digital identity solution, the Digital Certificate of Entitlement (DCE) for proof-of-life, represents a paradigm shift toward a secure, accessible, and user-controlled identity infrastructure. The DCE's design was shaped by a comprehensive risk management framework addressing business, governance, technology, and process aspects, and by the self-sovereign identity (SSI) paradigm, in which blockchain enables individuals to own and manage their identities independently via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials, rather than identities being controlled by central authorities. This architecture reduces the impact of data breaches (personal data is not centrally stored), eliminates single points of failure, and returns control of personal information to individuals.

chunks.heading: Foreword: accessibility, inclusion, and business impact
chunks.text: The DCE architecture incorporates biometric facial recognition and, for regions with limited connectivity, offline authentication capabilities using Kiosks installed in relevant United Nations field offices. The risk assessment methodology explicitly identified vulnerable populations — including remote and rural residents and individuals with low technical literacy — and implemented specific measures to ensure their inclusion. Cost reductions for UNJSPF are significant, from savings in printing, mailing, physical and logical archiving, and manual verification of signatures. The most profound impact is enabling over 70,000 UNJSPF clients to access and perform an essential activity with peace of mind, immediate notification, and confidence about the result.

chunks.heading: Executive summary
chunks.text: The white paper explores blockchain as a foundational infrastructure for digital identity management, using UNJSPF's Digital Certificate of Entitlement (DCE) as a case study. The DCE uses biometrics, artificial intelligence (AI), cryptographic validation, and secure geo-location data to modernize pension verification, replacing outdated paper-based processes. By adopting the DCE, UNJSPF has streamlined operations, reduced administrative costs, and implemented a tamper-proof system benefiting thousands of retirees from the UN and 24 other UNJSPF member organizations worldwide, while strengthening fraud prevention and improving regulatory compliance. The paper advocates for collaborative governance models and standardized frameworks to facilitate cross-agency adoption of UN blockchain identity solutions, contributing to SDG 16.9 and broader UN digital governance priorities.

chunks.part: What is Blockchain and Digital Identity
chunks.heading: Why blockchain for digital identity: five premises
chunks.text: Blockchain is presented as the ultimate technology for digital identity verification based on five premises: (1) Security and immutability — cryptographic mechanisms safeguard identity records from tampering and fraud once registered. (2) Decentralization and user control — moves control away from centralized institutions that can be compromised or misused. (3) Interoperability and seamless verification — open standards let organizations authenticate users without duplicating identity records, streamlining access to public services, financial institutions, and humanitarian programs. (4) Fraud prevention and identity theft protection — AI to fight deepfakes plus blockchain's decentralized structure reduce unauthorized access and identity cloning. (5) Privacy-preservation — Verifiable Credentials (VCs) allow secure proof of identity without exposing sensitive personal data.

chunks.part: What is Blockchain and Digital Identity
chunks.heading: Types of digital identity and the rise of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI)
chunks.text: The World Economic Forum defines three types of digital identity: centralized (owned/managed by a single organization), federated (third-party identity providers distribute information to other digital services), and decentralized (the owner manages their identity independently). Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) are globally unique identifiers created, owned, and controlled by the entity they represent, resolvable via a distributed ledger and verifiable cryptographically. Verifiable Credentials (VCs) are cryptographically verifiable digital statements made by an issuer about a subject (e.g. educational certificates, identity documents), tamper-evident and verifiable independently of the issuer. DIDs and VCs together gave rise to Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), standardized in part by the W3C, representing a shift from federated identity management toward individuals having complete sovereignty over their digital credentials and personal data.

chunks.part: What is Blockchain and Digital Identity
chunks.heading: Challenges blockchain-based digital identity addresses (and remaining challenges)
chunks.text: Blockchain-based digital public infrastructure addresses data breaches (by eliminating central points of failure), identity theft (cryptographic nature makes forging identities difficult), user privacy (users decide what information to share and with whom), and interoperability (seamless identity verification across platforms and organizations). However, implementation faces substantial challenges: complex governance decisions around the balance between privacy and transparency, significant technical hurdles transitioning from legacy systems, and equity challenges in ensuring universal access across different levels of technical literacy. Success depends on the right balance between decentralization and necessary oversight.

chunks.part: Practical Application at UN Joint Staff Pension Fund
chunks.heading: UNICC's role and the UNJSPF/UNICC/Hyperledger partnership
chunks.text: The United Nations International Computing Centre (UNICC), established in 1971, is the largest strategic partner for digital solutions and cybersecurity within the UN system, supporting over 100 partners and clients. UNICC previously explored blockchain-based digital solutions with UNHCR to support refugees. To assess blockchain's potential for digital identification in multi-national environments, UNICC and UNJSPF joined forces with the Hyperledger Foundation to improve and secure the UN pension process globally by putting a blockchain-supported digital identification infrastructure into production.

chunks.part: Practical Application at UN Joint Staff Pension Fund
chunks.heading: Why UNJSPF needed digital identification
chunks.text: UNJSPF's seven-decade-old manual proof-of-life verification process, covering beneficiaries in over 190 countries, was prone to human error, postal mail delays, and fraud; a single delayed verification or administrative error could suspend vital pension benefits. UNJSPF identified four critical pillars of a viable digital identity infrastructure: identity verification (working across borders and jurisdictions), existence verification (real-time digital confirmation replacing paper), transaction validation (an immutable digital record withstanding audit), and location verification (essential to the two-track system, which adjusts payments based on beneficiaries' residence).

chunks.part: Practical Application at UN Joint Staff Pension Fund
chunks.heading: Case: the traditional Certificate of Entitlement (CE) process
chunks.text: Beneficiaries receiving periodic benefits must annually submit a completed Certificate of Entitlement (CE) to UNJSPF to confirm their existence, a process in place for over 70 years, ensuring benefits are not paid to deceased individuals. The certificate includes the pension number and type of benefits and requires the retiree's signature or thumbprint. The Fund sends a barcoded certificate at the end of May (first CE mailing); if not returned within three months, a second mailing occurs in early September; the certificate must be received by year-end to avoid suspension. Beneficiaries not under the two-track system can access and submit certificates through Member Self-Service (MSS), by mail or digitally; those on the two-track cannot use MSS for this purpose since the Fund must verify declared residency. Submissions must be original or hand-signed scanned copies.

chunks.heading: Objectives of the blockchain-based digital identity system
chunks.text: The modernization challenge grew as UNJSPF's beneficiary base reached over 70,000 across 190 countries, requiring over 85,000 forms processed annually and causing approximately 1,400 annual payment suspensions due to delivery failures and signature verification issues (worsened by COVID-19 disruption of the mail-based system). Seven key objectives were identified: (1) Universal legal identity, aligned with SDG Target 16.9. (2) Decentralized identity management giving individuals control over personal data. (3) Operational efficiency across UN agencies and humanitarian operations. (4) Enhanced security and privacy leveraging blockchain's inherent security features. (5) Interoperability and standardization across agencies and programs. (6) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) integration. (7) Cross-border cooperation through standardized verification respecting local regulations and privacy laws.

chunks.heading: The case for blockchain application in the UN system
chunks.text: Blockchain addresses several current identification-system issues for the UN: data security (reduces risk of massive breaches by eliminating central points of failure), efficiency in operations (faster identity verification and authentication), cost management (lower operational costs allow more funds toward essential programs), preventing fraud (combats fraudulent digital identities), and transparency and accountability (an auditable trail of records deters fraud and corruption). More broadly for the UN ecosystem, blockchain also supports trust and reliability (automated data transparency reduces misinformation risk), regulatory compliance (aligning with UN Data Privacy Principles, closely aligned with GDPR), and identity accessibility (over 1 billion people globally lack proof of identity, hindering access to education, employment, government services, and financial resources).

chunks.heading: The DCE solution: design, security review, and privacy protections
chunks.text: The DCE is a biometric-based, secure, tamper-proof identity verification system powered by blockchain and AI, ensuring seamless validation of pension entitlements for retirees across the UN system and other UNJSPF member organizations. UNJSPF implemented comprehensive security protocols through independent expert assessments covering 11 critical domains (from network architecture to smart contract integrity), adhering to international ISO standards, alongside a parallel privacy assessment across policy, data management, and organizational frameworks. DCE incorporates AI to enhance biometric recognition, detecting and preventing deepfakes. All personal data remains securely stored on the user's device, with no sensitive information exchanged or centrally stored.

chunks.heading: DCE rollout timeline and adoption metrics
chunks.text: The DCE initiative began with a pilot in 2020, targeting 351 beneficiaries across 43 countries, in a two-phase rollout (May and June 2020) that allowed critical system optimization including enhanced security protocols and biometric interface improvements. Following successful pilot completion and board review, the solution was fully implemented in January 2021. After five years in production, over 43,000 beneficiaries were actively using the platform in 2025, accounting for 53% of the total beneficiary population. This digital transformation led to a 40% reduction in paper-based CE processing. The DCE's retention rate in 2024 was 99.96% — only 15 beneficiaries opted to return to paper-based processing despite the option being available to all.

chunks.heading: DCE additional verification capabilities: Proof-of-Transaction and Proof-of-Location
chunks.text: Beyond identity verification, the DCE solution uses blockchain, biometrics, and geo-location technologies to support additional verifications, including Proof-of-Transaction (an immutable digital record that can withstand scrutiny and audit) and Proof-of-Location (accurately delivering benefits under the two-track system, which adjusts payments based on the beneficiary's declared residence).

chunks.heading: Architecture: Hyperledger Indy and Aries
chunks.text: The DCE solution utilizes a permissioned blockchain identity system built on two Hyperledger Foundation frameworks: Indy and Aries. Hyperledger Indy provides decentralized identity management, storing critical cryptographic elements (public keys, verification proofs) to enable self-sovereign identity management and supporting Verifiable Credentials that let organizations issue, verify, and revoke digital credentials. The system operates through a distributed ledger structure with four components: a pool ledger (identifies network nodes), a domain ledger (maintains identity records), a configuration ledger (manages network parameters), and an audit ledger (ensures synchronization), operating under the Redundant Byzantine Fault Tolerance (RBFT) consensus protocol. Hyperledger Aries extends this with blockchain-agnostic protocols and an agent-based architecture facilitating interactions between credential holders, issuers, and verifiers.

chunks.heading: Architecture: issuers, holders, and verifiers
chunks.text: Issuers are responsible for generating and distributing Verifiable Credentials (VCs) to holders, defining schemas for common credential types and cryptographically signing credentials to ensure authenticity and integrity. Holders are entities who possess credentials, stored in digital wallets (cryptographically secured files acting like physical wallets); holders can selectively share credentials with verifiers through privacy-preserving mechanisms without needing a trusted third party or the issuer. Verifiers rely on blockchain transparency to independently validate credential authenticity without an intermediary, using Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP).

chunks.heading: Identity verification process (business logic)
chunks.text: The DCE mobile app is an end-user application that leverages AI identity verification technology to verify beneficiary liveness on the edge (locally), securing and processing the user's biometric footprint locally. The identity establishment process (one-time) involves liveness detection and presentation-attack verification leading to a biometric baseline, an established identity, and an onboarding verifiable credential generated after identity is verified over a video call. The identity verification process (once a year) involves biometric comparison against the baseline, leading to identity verified, an onboarding credential verifiable presentation, and finally a DCE credential issued — completed locally on the smartphone via an AI-assisted liveness check each year. Verifiable credentials (anoncreds) are stored in beneficiaries' custodial holder digital wallets, backed by a public permissioned blockchain running on a geographically distributed Hyperledger Indy ledger (nodes across America, Europe, Africa, UNICC datacenter, and public cloud).

chunks.heading: Adoption progress and elimination of paper certifications
chunks.text: Since implementation in 2021, the DCE has significantly reduced reliance on paper-based certification documents. Adoption reached 53% of beneficiaries by 2025, with gradual increase since the 2021 rollout, eliminating the need for paper certifications among registered DCE users. A key operational gain is in the signature verification process, where DCE-enrolled beneficiaries bypass traditional review requirements.

chunks.heading: Financial impact: overtime expense reduction
chunks.text: Prior to DCE implementation, UNJSPF processed more than 60,000 paper certifications annually, each requiring manual handling for opening, scanning, ERP system integration, and archiving. Analysis after four years of operation found overtime expenditures were lowered by 76.5% between 2021 and 2024. The most significant improvement occurred in the initial transition period: overtime expenses during the peak months of June through August dropped by 58.8% between 2021 and 2022. 2024 marked the lowest recorded overtime expenditure, representing less than a quarter (23.5%) of the 2021 baseline.

chunks.heading: Processing savings and printing reduction
chunks.text: In 2025, digital issuance reached over 38,800 certificates. Paper certificate printing was reduced to 36,852 in 2024, down from 64,443 in 2020 (the year before DCE was implemented) — an unprecedented reduction in printing levels even as the number of beneficiaries increased from approximately 65,000 to over 70,000. The substantial adoption of DCE by over 43,000 beneficiaries demonstrates strong acceptance of digital public infrastructure, generating measurable cost efficiencies through reduced paper form procurement and mailing expenses, while eliminating manual printing requirements for enrolled beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: Archiving expenditure reduction
chunks.text: Over a five-year period, archiving expenditures decreased by more than 95%. This reduction stems from two key innovations implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic: (1) introduction of email-based communication and a self-service portal for beneficiaries, and (2) the DCE solution, which eliminated the need for over 70,000 pieces of annual paper correspondence. Archiving costs dropped by roughly half or more each subsequent year, most dramatically between 2020 and 2021 (down 61%), then 76% between 2021 and 2022, followed by further reductions of 29% and 24% in subsequent years. Beneficiaries who complete their DCE verification before the first mailing cycle are automatically considered compliant with Proof-of-Life requirements, eliminating the need for paper documentation entirely.

chunks.heading: Signature verification cost reduction
chunks.text: The DCE solution completely reorganized signature verification workflows through the Automatic Signature Verification system, prompted in part by internal audit recommendations. Even as the verification scope expanded to encompass all beneficiaries, the DCE has proven remarkably scalable, processing verification requests for the beneficiary base exceeding 70,000 with minimal additional resource investment. Cases still requiring attention (e.g., involving thumbprints or additional documentation), which once consumed hours of staff time, now require just a fraction of that time due to digital workflows.

chunks.heading: Fraud prevention via biometric authentication and location data
chunks.text: AI-based biometric authentication has markedly enhanced security protocols, offering substantially more protection against fraud and overpayments compared to traditional signature-based systems. Beneficiaries undergo an initial enrolment phase, followed by a direct video consultation with a Digital CE agent who assesses eligibility against predetermined criteria; upon approval, the system creates a secure biometric profile that serves as the benchmark for all future transactions. The security framework also requires precise location data during DCE issuance, maintaining strict oversight of residency requirements — a critical component of the two-track system. The personal nature of biometric data ensures only authorized beneficiaries can access the system, preventing unauthorized usage and fraudulent benefit claims.

chunks.heading: Path forward: DCE as a multi-agency consortium / digital public good
chunks.text: The DCE is envisioned as a digital public good, offered as 'DCE-as-a-Service' to other international organizations via a multi-agency consortium, in line with the UN Digital Compact (enhanced digital cooperation and shared governance) and the Pact for the Future (collective action, inclusivity, and digital trust). It is intended to be offered as a ready-to-use Software-as-a-Service solution, with the consortium operationalizing the service delivery model and cost-sharing mechanisms among international organizations.

chunks.heading: DCE consortium key pillars and principles
chunks.text: The DCE consortium model, established by agreement among founding members, adheres to key pillars: UN Shared Service (aligned with the UN Mutual Recognition Declaration, leveraging economies of scale among UN and Multilateral Development Banks); Cost recovery and sharing (a full cost recovery and sharing model distributing maintenance/upgrade fees equitably); Governance framework and onboarding (defining rules of engagement, operational models with service level agreements, roles and responsibilities); Steering group for joint decision-making (consortium members participate in strategic decisions including new capabilities); and Evolution and innovation (continuous improvement, monitoring technology trends). Overarching principles include equitable contribution and scalability (larger entities contribute proportionally more), flexibility and transparency (clear cost calculation guidelines), sustainability (adequate cost coverage for maintenance/upgrades), and governance oversight (robust mechanisms overseeing the cost-sharing framework).

chunks.heading: Consortium operating model: costs
chunks.text: UNICC will serve as a trusted IT partner implementing configuration and integrations with a partner organization's back-end systems (e.g., ERP). The DCE Consortium's operating model consists of two primary components designed to ensure scalability and sustainability: one-time onboarding costs (full configuration of the DCE plus an onboarding nominal fee) and recurring operational support costs.
